items.title: The damped driven oscillator model: second-order equation, phase-plane system and characteristic data
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k\in\mathbb R$ be given real numbers, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). The **damped driven oscillator model** with data $(m,c,k,f)$ is the second-order equation

$$m\,x''(t)+c\,x'(t)+k\,x(t)=f(t),\qquad t\in I .$$

A **solution** of the model on an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior is a twice differentiable $x:J\to\mathbb R$ such that the identity holds for every $t\in J$, derivatives being ordinary real derivatives ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The model is called **homogeneous** when $f\equiv 0$, **undamped** when $c=0$, and **strictly damped** when $c>0$.

The **phase-plane equation** of the model has right-hand side

$$G_f:I\times\mathbb R^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^2,\qquad G_f(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \frac{f(t)-c\,v-k\,x}{m}\Bigr).$$

Here $\mathbb R^2$ is the **phase plane**, with coordinates $(x,v)$, where $x$ is the **displacement** and $v$ the **velocity**. For an interval $J\subseteq I$ with nonempty interior, a differentiable curve $z=(x,v):J\to\mathbb R^2$ solves the phase-plane equation when $z'(t)=G_f(t,z(t))$ for every $t\in J$, using the domain-relative derivative at any included endpoint ([[def-derivative]]). If $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$, then $t\mapsto(x(t),x'(t))$ solves this equation; conversely, if $t\mapsto(x(t),v(t))$ solves it, then $v=x'$ and $x$ is a solution of the model on $J$. When $J$ is open, this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $J\times\mathbb R^2$. For the homogeneous model the right-hand side is written $G_0(x,v)=(v,-(cv+kx)/m)$.

The **characteristic polynomial** of the model is

$$p(\lambda):=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k,$$

with **discriminant** $\Delta:=c^2-4mk$. When $k>0$ define the **undamped frequency** $\omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}$, the **damping rate** $\gamma:=c/(2m)$ and, when $4mk>c^2$, the **damped frequency** $\omega:=\sqrt{k/m-\gamma^2}=\sqrt{4mk-c^2}/(2m)$; the corresponding square roots are the nonnegative real ones.
items.strategy: Define the model, its solution notion, the phase-plane reduction and the characteristic data with explicit domains and regularity; no existence or uniqueness claim is smuggled into the definition.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.1)-(5.13a): harmonic oscillator, linear drag force, damping coefficient and the forced equation $m\ddot q+\eta\dot q+\kappa q=F(t)$; printed pages 1-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 87-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.15): the linearised forced damped oscillator and the underdamped, critically damped and overdamped solution cases, printed pages 147-148

items.title: Periodic averaging data: the average field, the oscillatory part and the periodic deviation
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $P>0$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). Assume that for each standard coordinate vector $e_j$ of $\mathbb R^n$, $0\le j<n$, and every $(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times O$, the vector-valued derivative at $r=0$ of $r\mapsto f(t,x+r e_j)$ exists, and that each resulting partial derivative $(t,x)\mapsto\partial_{x_j}f(t,x)$ is continuous on $\mathbb R\times O$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). This is the meaning of **continuously partially differentiable in the state variable** here. Suppose also that $f$ is **$P$-periodic in time**, that is

$$f(t+P,x)=f(t,x)\qquad\text{for all }(t,x)\in\mathbb R\times O .$$

The **average** of such an $f$ is the map

$$\bar f:O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad \bar f(x):=\frac1P\int_0^Pf(s,x)\,ds,$$

where the integral is the componentwise Riemann integral of the continuous curve $s\mapsto f(s,x)$ over the compact interval $[0,P]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-interval]]); it is well defined and finite for every $x\in O$ by componentwise application of [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. The **oscillatory part** of $f$ is $f-\bar f$, and the **deviation** of $f$ is

$$g:[0,P]\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad g(t,x):=\int_0^t\bigl(f(s,x)-\bar f(x)\bigr)\,ds .$$

Because $\int_0^Pf(s,x)-\bar f(x)\,ds=P\bar f(x)-P\bar f(x)=0$ by the linearity clause of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] and the componentwise constant-integral formula of [[lem-integral-elementary-bounds]], the formula $g(t+kP,x):=g(t,x)$ for $k\in\mathbb Z$ and $t\in[0,P)$ defines a unique extension, again written $g$, to all of $\mathbb R\times O$; it satisfies $g(t+P,x)=g(t,x)$ and $g(0,x)=0$ for all $(t,x)$, and on $[0,P]$ it is the integral displayed above.

The **averaged (or reduced) system** of $f$ for a parameter $\varepsilon>0$ is the autonomous first-order system on $O$

$$y'(t)=\varepsilon\,\bar f(y(t)).$$
items.strategy: Introduce the averaging objects by explicit formulas and state the periodic extension's well-definedness conditions; all bounds are proved separately.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57): harmonic balance and the reduced (RWA) equations obtained by time averaging over one period, printed pages 12-14 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 99-101)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.25)-(5.28): averaging the first-order perturbation over one period and the secular change of the averaged variable, printed pages 95-98

items.title: A one-frequency parameter-dependent action-angle branch, its transformed Hamiltonian and its drift generator
items.statement:
Let $\varepsilon>0$, let $\widehat J,\widehat S\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open intervals, and let $J\subseteq\widehat J$ and $S\subseteq\widehat S$ be intervals with nonempty interiors ([[def-interval]]). Let $h:\widehat J\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R$ and $k:\widehat J\times\mathbb R\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$ on these open Euclidean domains ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and suppose $k$ is $2\pi$-periodic in its second variable on $J\times\mathbb R\times S$:

$$k(I,\theta+2\pi,s)=k(I,\theta,s)\qquad\text{for all }(I,\theta,s)\in J\times\mathbb R\times S .$$

The **transformed Hamiltonian** of the datum is

$$K(I,\theta,s):=h(I,s)+\varepsilon\,k(I,\theta,s),$$

its **frequency function** is

$$\omega(I,s):=\partial_Ih(I,s),$$

its **angle average** is $\langle k\rangle(I,s):=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}k(I,\theta,s)\,d\theta$, and, on the set where $\omega\ne0$, its **drift generator** is

$$g(I,\theta,s):=\frac{k(I,\theta,s)-\langle k\rangle(I,s)}{\omega(I,s)} .$$

The **branch vector field** of the datum is the restriction to $J\times\mathbb R\times S$ of the map $\widehat\Phi:\widehat J\times\mathbb R\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R^3$,

$$\widehat\Phi(I,\theta,s):=\Bigl(-\varepsilon\,\partial_\theta k(I,\theta,s),\ \ \partial_Ih(I,s)+\varepsilon\,\partial_Ik(I,\theta,s),\ \ \varepsilon\Bigr),$$

and a **branch solution** on an interval $T\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a differentiable $(I,\theta,s):T\to J\times\mathbb R\times S$ satisfying $(I,\theta,s)'=\widehat\Phi(I,\theta,s)$ at every $t\in T$, with derivatives relative to $T$ at included endpoints. On open time intervals this is the first-order system of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]] on the open domain $\widehat J\times\mathbb R\times\widehat S$ ([[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]). Partial derivatives are those of the ambient Euclidean coordinates.
items.strategy: Define the branch datum, its drift generator and its vector field explicitly; the existence of such a chart for a given family is left as a consumer hypothesis.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 4.6, Eqs. (4.149)-(4.158): the action $I=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,dq$ of a one-dimensional family with slow parameter $\lambda(t)$ and the averaged statement $\langle\dot I\rangle=0$, printed pages 113-115

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3, Eqs. (10.28)-(10.42): action variable $J=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,dq$, the averaged energy-change identity and the adiabatic-invariance conclusion $J=\text{const}$, printed pages 5-8 of Chapter 10 (PDF pages 241-244)

items.title: Differentiation of a variable-limit convolution integral with a C-one matrix kernel
items.reference: batch-7-local-construction; a necessary mathematical prerequisite added by this scaffolder and recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, equip $\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $t_0\in I$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval with $I-I:=\{t-s:t,s\in I\}\subseteq U$, let $g:U\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ have $C^1$ entries ([[def-matrix-space]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). For $B=(b_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, define $(Bv)_i:=\sum_{j<n}b_{ij}v_j$. This is a linear map by the coordinate formula; the Euclidean norm is a norm by [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], and the standard coordinate vectors form an ordered basis by [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]], so the map is bounded by [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]]. Let $\|B\|$ denote its induced operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). All matrix actions in the integrals use this convention. Since $0\in I-I\subseteq U$, the value $g(0)$ is defined. Define

$$F:I\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad F(t):=\int_{t_0}^t g(t-s)f(s)\,ds,$$

with the oriented integral of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] and the matrix action just defined; the integrand is continuous in $s$, hence integrable on every compact subinterval. Then:

1. $F$ is differentiable at every interior point $t$ of $I$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(t)=g(0)f(t)+\int_{t_0}^t g'(t-s)f(s)\,ds .$$

2. If moreover $g'$ is bounded on compact subintervals of $U$ (which holds automatically because $g$ is $C^1$), then $F$ is of class $C^1$ on the interior of $I$.
items.strategy: Split the difference quotient into a parameter-derivative term over a fixed interval, handled by differentiation under the integral sign, and a moving-endpoint term, handled by uniform continuity; then prove continuity of the derivative.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (retrieved 365-page online edition), Section 3.1, printed pp. 59-61 (matrix action and exponential), and Section 3.4, Theorem 3.12, printed pp. 83-84 (variation of constants). The convolution derivative is proved locally.
J. Lebl, Basic Analysis I, Section 8.4 (the second fundamental theorem of calculus and differentiation of parameter integrals), online text

items.title: The homogeneous damped oscillator: solution classification by the discriminant and uniqueness for initial data
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$ and $k>0$, and consider the homogeneous damped oscillator model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero, with characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda)=m\lambda^2+c\lambda+k$, discriminant $\Delta=c^2-4mk$, damping rate $\gamma:=c/(2m)$, and, when applicable, roots
$$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt\Delta}{2m}\ (\Delta\ge0),\qquad \lambda:=-\frac{c}{2m},\qquad \omega:=\frac{\sqrt{4mk-c^2}}{2m}\ (\Delta<0).$$

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Distinct real roots.** If $\Delta>0$, then $\lambda_+>\lambda_-$ are exactly the real roots of $p$, and a function $x:J\to\mathbb R$ on an interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior is a solution of the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

2. **Double real root.** If $\Delta=0$, then $\lambda=-c/(2m)$ is the only root of $p$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=(A+Bt)e^{\lambda t}\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

3. **Complex conjugate roots.** If $\Delta<0$, then $\omega>0$, the roots of $p$ are $-\gamma\pm i\omega$, and $x:J\to\mathbb R$ is a solution if and only if
$$x(t)=e^{-\gamma t}\bigl(A\cos(\omega t)+B\sin(\omega t)\bigr)\quad(t\in J)$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$.

4. **Initial data.** In each of the three cases and for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ there is exactly one solution $x:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x'(0)=v_0$. Its coefficients are
$$A=\frac{v_0-\lambda_-x_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-},\quad B=\frac{\lambda_+x_0-v_0}{\lambda_+-\lambda_-}\quad(\Delta>0),\qquad A=x_0,\ B=v_0-\lambda x_0\quad(\Delta=0),$$
$$A=x_0,\quad B=\frac{v_0+\gamma x_0}{\omega}\quad(\Delta<0).$$
items.strategy: Verify each family by direct differentiation (using the complex exponential in the oscillatory case), match initial data by explicit linear algebra, and prove exhaustiveness by a connectedness argument using the local uniqueness lemma for the phase-plane field.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.6)-(5.12): characteristic equation $\lambda^2+2\delta\lambda+\omega_0^2=0$, its roots (5.8) and the free solution (5.9); printed pages 2-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 88-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16): underdamped, critically damped and overdamped solution cases of the linearised oscillator, printed page 148

G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (retrieved 365-page online edition), Section 3.1, printed pp. 59-61 (matrix exponential). The three scalar families and their exhaustiveness are verified locally from the declared mathematical suppliers.

items.title: The degenerate and repulsive oscillator: solutions for k=0 and the explicit growing solution for k<0
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, let $k\le0$, and consider the model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=0$ of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ identically zero. In the three cases below, $x:J\to\mathbb R$ runs over solutions on intervals $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior.

A local solution here may have any interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior, with domain-relative derivatives at included endpoints. It has a unique extension to the global family below. A **maximal solution** means one that has no solution extension to a strictly larger interval; the maximal solutions of this global autonomous equation are precisely the family members on $\mathbb R$. For a homogeneous model restricted to a time domain $I$, its solutions have $J\subseteq I$ and are restrictions of these same global members; their extensions solve the all-$\mathbb R$ equation.

1. **Double zero root ($k=0$, $c=0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if $x(t)=A+Bt$ for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely $x(t)=x_0+v_0t$.
2. **Simple zero root ($k=0$, $c>0$).** Then on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=A+Be^{-ct/m}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a unique global member of this family. For every datum $(x_0,v_0)$ there is a unique global solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, namely the member with $A=x_0+\frac{m v_0}{c}$ and $B=-\frac{m v_0}{c}$. This global solution has limit $A$ as $t\to+\infty$; any local solution on an interval unbounded above has the same limit along that interval.
3. **One positive and one negative root ($k<0$).** Put $$\lambda_\pm:=\frac{-c\pm\sqrt{c^2-4mk}}{2m}.$$ Then $\lambda_-<0<\lambda_+$, both are real roots of the characteristic polynomial, and on every such interval $J$, $x$ solves the model if and only if
$$x(t)=Ae^{\lambda_+t}+Be^{\lambda_-t}$$
for some $A,B\in\mathbb R$; each such local solution is the restriction of a global member of this family. In particular the global solution $t\mapsto e^{\lambda_+t}$ has data $x(0)=1$, $x'(0)=\lambda_+$ and satisfies $e^{\lambda_+t}\to+\infty$ as $t\to+\infty$: the model has an unbounded solution growing exponentially on $[0,\infty)$.
items.strategy: Derive the k=0 families by integrating the first-order equation for x'; verify the exponential solutions for k<0, exhibit the growing solution, and obtain uniqueness from the local uniqueness lemma.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.6)-(5.9): characteristic equation and the free damped solutions, including the high-damping and free cases, printed pages 2-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 88-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16) and the surrounding classification of linearised oscillator solutions, printed page 148

items.title: Variation of constants for $z'=Az+b(t)$ via the matrix exponential
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, equip $\mathbb R^n$ with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], let $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]), let $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$, and let $b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The Euclidean norm is a norm by [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], and the standard coordinate vectors form an ordered basis by [[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]. For $A=(a_{ij})$ and $z\in\mathbb R^n$, define $(Az)_i:=\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}z_j$; this is a linear map by [[def-linear-map]], hence bounded by [[cor-linear-maps-with-finite-dimensional-domain-are-bounded]], and $\|A\|$ denotes its induced Euclidean operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Matrix powers and products use [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]; their action agrees with composition of the corresponding linear maps by distributing the finite sums in the displayed coordinate formula. Define the **matrix exponential**

$$E:\mathbb R\longrightarrow M_n(\mathbb R),\qquad E(t):=\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{t^k}{k!}A^k .$$

Then:

1. $E$ is well defined and of class $C^1$, with $E(0)=I_n$, $E(u+v)=E(u)E(v)$, $\frac{d}{du}E(u)=AE(u)=E(u)A$ for all $u,v\in\mathbb R$, and $\|E(u)\|\le e^{\|A\||u|}$ for the operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]) subordinate to the Euclidean norm.
2. The map
$$z:\mathbb R\longrightarrow\mathbb R^n,\qquad z(t):=E(t-t_0)z_0+\int_{t_0}^tE(t-s)b(s)\,ds,$$
satisfies $z(t_0)=z_0$ and $z'(t)=A\,z(t)+b(t)$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$.
3. Uniqueness: if $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ is an interval with nonempty interior containing $t_0$ ([[def-interval]]) and $w:J\to\mathbb R^n$ is differentiable with $w'=Aw+b$ on $J$ and $w(t_0)=z_0$, then $w=z|_J$.
items.strategy: Combine the exponential-series lemma with the convolution differentiation lemma to verify the explicit solution, and prove uniqueness by Gronwall.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (retrieved 365-page online edition), Section 3.1, Eqs. (3.2)-(3.12), printed pp. 59-61; Section 3.4, Theorem 3.12, Eq. (3.97), printed pp. 83-84.

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.27)-(5.30): the temporal Green's function as the response to a short pulse, $q(t)=\int f(t')G(t-t')\,dt'$, printed pages 6-7 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 92-93)

items.title: Strictly damped homogeneous oscillator with $k>0$: every solution tends to zero
items.strategy: Read the three explicit families off the classification theorem, bound them by the sign of the roots and the range of sine and cosine, and take the limits (including the t e^{lambda t} case by an exponential-series lower bound).

(5.9)-(5.12): exponential decay of the free damped oscillations with time constant $\tau=1/\delta$ and the quality factor, printed pages 2-3 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 88-89)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 7 Section 7.1.3, Eq. (7.16): the transient term of the linearised oscillator decays away exponentially, printed page 148

items.title: The forced oscillator with $k\ge0$: unique global solution and the convolution (Green's function) formula
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $c\ge0$, $k\ge0$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]) and let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Fix $t_0\in I$ and data $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$. Let $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be the (unique) solution of the associated homogeneous model with time domain $\mathbb R$ and zero forcing, with $g(0)=0$ and $g'(0)=1/m$.

Then:

1. There is exactly one solution $x:I\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with $x(t_0)=x_0$ and $x'(t_0)=v_0$. It is twice differentiable on $I$, with derivatives at included endpoints taken relative to $I$, and $x''$ is continuous on $I$ in its relative topology.
2. If $x_h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ is any homogeneous solution with $x_h(t_0)=x_0$ and $x_h'(t_0)=v_0$ (it exists and is unique by [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] and [[prop-cm-oscillator-degenerate-and-repulsive-cases]]), then
$$x(t)=x_h(t)+\int_{t_0}^tg(t-s)f(s)\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$
items.strategy: Construct the solution as homogeneous part plus convolution, verify the equation by two applications of the convolution lemma using g''=-(c g'+k g)/m, and invoke the variation-of-constants uniqueness.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.13)-(5.18) and (5.27)-(5.30): the forced equation, the response function and the temporal Green's function $q(t)=\int f(t')G(t-t')\,dt'$, printed pages 3-7 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 89-93)

G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (retrieved 365-page online edition), Section 3.4, Theorem 3.12 and Eqs. (3.92)-(3.97), printed pp. 83-84 (continuous inhomogeneous linear forcing).

items.title: Forced quadratic system $Mq''+Kq=\varphi(t)$: decoupled forced modes and the convolution solution
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $M\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric positive definite, let $K\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ be symmetric and non-negative, let $S:=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}=O\Lambda O^{\mathsf T}$ with $O$ orthogonal and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, $\lambda_i\ge0$ ([[thm-cm-quadratic-mode-decomposition]]), let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and let $t_0\in I$. Put

$$\psi(t):=O^{\mathsf T}M^{-1/2}\varphi(t),\qquad \omega_i:=\sqrt{\lambda_i}\ (\lambda_i>0),$$

and for a curve $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ whose first and second derivatives exist on $I$ (relative to $I$ at included endpoints) and whose second derivative is continuous on $I$, put $z:=O^{\mathsf T}M^{1/2}q$. Then:

1. $q$ solves the forced quadratic system $Mq''+Kq=\varphi$ on $I$ if and only if $z$ solves the decoupled forced system
$$z_i''+\lambda_iz_i=\psi_i\qquad(1\le i\le n)$$
on $I$.
2. For each $i$, the unique solution $z_i:I\to\mathbb R$ of the scalar equation in clause 1 with data $z_i(t_0)=\xi_i$, $z_i'(t_0)=\eta_i$ is
$$z_i(t)=\xi_i\cos\bigl(\omega_i(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac{\eta_i}{\omega_i}\sin\bigl(\omega_i(t-t_0)\bigr)+\frac1{\omega_i}\int_{t_0}^t\sin\bigl(\omega_i(t-s)\bigr)\psi_i(s)\,ds\quad(\lambda_i>0),$$
$$z_i(t)=\xi_i+\eta_i(t-t_0)+\int_{t_0}^t(t-s)\psi_i(s)\,ds\quad(\lambda_i=0).$$
3. Consequently, for every initial datum $(q(t_0),q'(t_0))\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ there is exactly one solution $q:I\to\mathbb R^n$ of $Mq''+Kq=\varphi$ with that datum, and it is $q=M^{-1/2}Oz$ for the $z$ of clause 2.
items.strategy: Transport the forced system through the modal transformation of the quadratic-mode theorem and apply the scalar forced-oscillator theorem mode by mode.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (retrieved 365-page online edition), Section 8.4, Eqs. items.title: Sinusoidal forcing: the steady response, its amplitude and phase, and resonance at $\Omega=\sqrt{k/m}$
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c\ge0$, let $f_0\in\mathbb R$ and $\Omega\ge0$, and consider the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f$ with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and forcing $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(t)=f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). Put

$$D:=k-m\Omega^2+i\,c\,\Omega\in\mathbb C,\qquad \omega_0:=\sqrt{k/m}.$$

1. **Non-resonant response.** If $D\ne0$, then the function
$$x_p(t):=\operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{f_0e^{i\Omega t}}{D}\right)=f_0\,\frac{(k-m\Omega^2)\cos(\Omega t)+c\,\Omega\sin(\Omega t)}{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$. Its amplitude about zero is $|f_0|/\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}$.

2. **Resonance.** If $c=0$ and $\Omega=\omega_0$, then $D=0$ and
$$x_p(t):=\frac{f_0\,t\sin(\omega_0t)}{2m\omega_0}$$
is a solution of the forced model on all of $\mathbb R$; if $f_0\ne0$ then $x_p$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.

3. **Transient decay.** If $c>0$, then $D\ne0$ for every $\Omega\ge0$, and every solution $x:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ of the forced model satisfies
$$x(t)=x_p(t)+x_h(t)$$
where $x_h$ is a homogeneous solution; consequently $x(t)-x_p(t)\to0$ as $t\to+\infty$ ([[def-limits-at-infinity]]) and $x$ is bounded on $[0,\infty)$.
items.strategy: Verify the complex ansatz and take real parts, verify the resonant solution directly and exhibit its unbounded sequence, and use the linear splitting plus the homogeneous decay corollary for the transient statement.

(5.14)-(5.22): the response function, the forced amplitude (5.18), the resonance value (5.19) and the resonance discussion, printed pages 3-5 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 89-91)

items.title: The amplitude of the sinusoidally forced damped oscillator: location and value of its maximum
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $k>0$, $c>0$ and $f_0\ne0$. For $\Omega\ge0$ let

$$A(\Omega):=\frac{|f_0|}{\sqrt{(k-m\Omega^2)^2+c^2\Omega^2}}$$

be the amplitude about zero of the steady response of [[thm-cm-forced-oscillator-sinusoidal-response]] clause 1, and put

$$u_*:=\frac{k}{m}-\frac{c^2}{2m^2},\qquad \Omega_*:=\sqrt{u_*}\ \ \text{when }u_*>0 .$$

Then:

1. If $u_*>0$ (equivalently $c^2<2mk$), $A$ is strictly increasing on $[0,\Omega_*]$, strictly decreasing on $[\Omega_*,\infty)$, and its maximum on $[0,\infty)$ is attained at $\Omega_*$ and at no other point, with
$$A(\Omega_*)=\frac{2m|f_0|}{c\sqrt{4mk-c^2}} .$$
2. If $u_*\le0$ then $A$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\infty)$ and its maximum on $[0,\infty)$ is attained at $\Omega=0$ and at no other point.
items.strategy: Write the denominator as an exact square m^2(u-u_*)^2+c^2(4mk-c^2)/(4m^2) in u=Omega^2, locate the vertex, and convert the monotonicity through the strictly decreasing maps x->1/x and x->sqrt(x).

items.title: Elementary bounds for the periodic average, the deviation and its time derivative
items.reference: batch-7-local-construction; a necessary mathematical prerequisite added by this scaffolder and recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $P>0$, $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ open, and let $f:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, continuously partially differentiable in the second variable and $P$-periodic in time, with average $\bar f$, oscillatory part $f-\bar f$ and periodic deviation $g$ as in [[def-cm-averaging-data-and-averaged-field]] ([[def-interval]]). Here $D_xf(t,x):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ denotes the total derivative in the state variable, with coordinate columns $\partial_{x_j}f(t,x)$; it exists and is continuous by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]. The same notation is used for $D_x\bar f$ and $D_xg$ when those total derivatives exist. Let $x_0\in O$, $R>0$ with $\overline B(x_0,R)\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) and let $M,L\ge0$ satisfy

$$\|f(t,x)\|_2\le M,\qquad \|f(t,x)-f(t,y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2\qquad(t\in\mathbb R,\ x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)).$$

Then:

1. $\|\bar f(x)\|_2\le M$ and $\|\bar f(x)-\bar f(y)\|_2\le L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)$.
2. $g$ is $P$-periodic and $\|g(t,x)\|_2\le2MP$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$ and $x\in\overline B(x_0,R)$; moreover $\|g(t,x)-g(t,y)\|_2\le2LP\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$ and $x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)$.
3. $\partial_tg(t,x)=f(t,x)-\bar f(x)$ for every $(t,x)$; consequently $\|\partial_tg(t,x)\|_2\le2M$ for $x\in\overline B(x_0,R)$ and $\|\partial_tg(t,x)-\partial_tg(t,y)\|_2\le2L\|x-y\|_2$ for all $t\in\mathbb R$ and $x,y\in\overline B(x_0,R)$.
4. $g$ has continuous first partial derivatives on $\mathbb R\times O$; its partial derivative in the second variable is $D_xg(t,x)=\int_0^t\bigl(D_xf(s,x)-D_x\bar f(x)\bigr)ds$, and $\|D_xg(t,x)\|\le2LP$ for $t\in\mathbb R$, $x\in\overline B(x_0,R)$, with $\|\cdot\|$ the operator norm on $M_n(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-operator-norm]]). In particular $g$ is totally differentiable at every point of $\mathbb R\times O$ ([[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]]).
items.strategy: Estimate the integrals with the norm inequality and monotonicity, control the time derivative by the fundamental theorem and periodicity at multiples of P, and obtain the state derivative by differentiation under the integral sign.

items.title: Finite-time linearization error bound: quadratic remainder, exponential growth bound and the variation-of-constants estimate
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $0\in U$, let $F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $r>0$, $C\ge0$, $L\ge0$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\overline B(0,r)\subseteq U$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) and

$$\|F(z)-Az\|_2\le C\|z\|_2^2,\qquad \|F(z)\|_2\le L\|z\|_2\qquad(\|z\|_2\le r),$$
where $Az$ and $\|A\|$ use the matrix-action and induced Euclidean operator-norm convention of [[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]].

Let $z_0\in\mathbb R^n$ with $\delta:=\|z_0\|_2>0$, let $T>0$ with $\delta e^{LT}<r$, and let $y:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^n$ be the solution of the linear system $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$ ([[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]]). Then:

1. The maximal solution $z$ of $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$ is defined on $[0,T]$ and satisfies $\|z(t)\|_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ for $t\in[0,T]$ ([[def-maximal-ode-solution]]).
2. For every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$\|z(t)-y(t)\|_2\le C\delta^2\int_0^te^{\|A\|(t-s)}e^{2Ls}\,ds\le C\delta^2\,t\,e^{(\|A\|+2L)t},$$
where $\|A\|$ is the operator norm of $A$ for the Euclidean norm ([[def-operator-norm]]).
items.strategy: Bound the maximal solution by Gronwall while it stays in the ball, extend it to [0,T] by compact continuation, and compare it with the linear solution by the variation-of-constants formula.

The explicit quadratic error estimate is derived locally.

items.title: Averaging for fast periodic oscillations: order-$\varepsilon$ agreement on the $O(1/\varepsilon)$ time scale
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, $P>0$, let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, continuously partially differentiable in the second variable and $P$-periodic in time, with average $\bar f$ and deviation $g$ as in [[def-cm-averaging-data-and-averaged-field]]. Here $D_xf(t,x)$ is the total derivative in the state variable defined in [[lem-cm-averaging-data-basic-bounds]]. Let $x_0\in O$, let $0<\rho<R$ with $\overline B(x_0,R)\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let $M,L\ge0$ satisfy

$$\|f(t,x)\|_2\le M,\qquad \|D_xf(t,x)\|\le L\qquad\bigl(t\in\mathbb R,\ x\in\overline B(x_0,R)\bigr),$$

$\|\cdot\|$ being the operator norm ([[def-operator-norm]]). Put

$$B:=2MP,\qquad B_1:=2LP,\qquad K:=e^{LA}\bigl[B+(LB+B_1M)A\bigr],$$

where $\varepsilon>0$ and $A>0$ are parameters. Suppose $y:[0,A/\varepsilon]\to\overline B(x_0,R-\rho)$ is a solution of the averaged system

$$y'(t)=\varepsilon\bar f(y(t)),\qquad y(0)=x_0 .$$

If $\varepsilon K<\rho$, then the solution $x$ of $x'(t)=\varepsilon f(t,x(t))$, $x(0)=x_0$ exists on all of $[0,A/\varepsilon]$ and satisfies, for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$,

$$\|x(t)-y(t)\|_2\le\varepsilon K=\varepsilon\,e^{LA}\bigl[B+(LB+B_1M)A\bigr].$$
items.strategy: Conjugate x by the deviation g to cancel the oscillatory term exactly, apply Gronwall to the resulting difference with y, and use the smallness condition to prevent exit from the trapping ball.

items.title: Adiabatic action drift bound: order-$\varepsilon$ change of the action on the $O(1/\varepsilon)$ time scale
items.statement:
Let $\varepsilon>0$, $A>0$, $\omega_0>0$, let $\widehat J,\widehat S\subseteq\mathbb R$ be open intervals, and let $J\subseteq\widehat J$ and $S\subseteq\widehat S$ be intervals with nonempty interiors ([[def-cm-parameter-dependent-action-angle-branch]], [[def-interval]]). Let $h:\widehat J\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R$ and $k:\widehat J\times\mathbb R\times\widehat S\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$, with $k$ $2\pi$-periodic in $\theta$ on $J\times\mathbb R\times S$. Let $K\subseteq J$ and $S_0\subseteq S$ be compact intervals, let $s_0\in S_0$, and suppose

$$|\partial_Ih(I,s)|\ge\omega_0\qquad\bigl((I,s)\in K\times S_0\bigr).$$

Let $(I,\theta,s):[0,A/\varepsilon]\to J\times\mathbb R\times S$ be a branch solution of the branch vector field of the datum ([[def-cm-parameter-dependent-action-angle-branch]]) with $s(0)=s_0$, and suppose that for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$ one has $I(t)\in K$ and $s(t)\in S_0$. Then for every $t\in[0,A/\varepsilon]$,

$$|I(t)-I(0)|\le\varepsilon\Bigl[2\sup_{K\times[0,2\pi]\times S_0}|g|+A\sup_{K\times[0,2\pi]\times S_0}\bigl|\partial_Ig\,\partial_\theta k-\partial_\theta g\,\partial_Ik-\partial_sg\bigr|\Bigr],$$

where $g=(k-\langle k\rangle)/\partial_Ih$ is the drift generator of the datum.
items.strategy: Compute the exact chain-rule identity (I+epsilon g)'=epsilon^2(partial_I g partial_theta k - partial_theta g partial_I k - partial_s g), integrate it over the horizon, and bound the two error terms.

items.title: Scope and limits of the oscillator, linearization, averaging and adiabatic items on this page
items.statement:
Every item on this page is mathematics: parameters, forcing functions, initial data and error constants are mathematical objects, and none of the statements asserts a physical law, a unit convention or an empirical fact. The following limits are part of the claims and must be carried by any consumer.

- **Linear oscillator results are exact for the stated model only.** [[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]] and [[prop-cm-oscillator-degenerate-and-repulsive-cases]] classify all solutions of the constant-coefficient model with the stated parameter ranges ($k>0$, resp. $k\le0$) and are exact equivalences, including the free zero mode when $k=0$ and the exponential growth when $k<0$. [[cor-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-decay]] needs $c>0$ and $k>0$; for $c=0$ no decay is claimed. [[thm-cm-forced-oscillator-variation-of-constants]] gives the exact convolution representation for continuous forcing and $k\ge0$; the kernel formula is a formula for that model, not a physical superposition principle. [[thm-cm-forced-oscillator-sinusoidal-response]] separates the steady response from the homogeneous transient; the resonant clause supplies an exact solution of the undamped resonant model, unbounded when $f_0\ne0$ and identically zero when $f_0=0$, and [[prop-cm-oscillator-amplitude-maximum]] locates the unique maximum of the response amplitude for $c>0$ and $f_0\ne0$ (for $c=0$ and $f_0\ne0$ the non-resonant amplitude is unbounded near $\omega_0$; for $f_0=0$ it is zero wherever its formula is defined). [[cor-cm-forced-modal-oscillator-response]] is exact for constant coefficient matrices $M,K$ and continuous forcing; it asserts nothing about nonlinear systems or configuration-dependent $M$.
- **Finite-time linearization is not a stability statement.** [[thm-cm-finite-time-linearization-error-bound]] is conditional on the explicit smallness condition $\delta e^{LT}<r$ and on a quadratic remainder bound on the ball, and concludes only $|z(t)-y(t)|=O(\delta^2)$ on the finite horizon $[0,T]$. It neither asserts long-time agreement of the nonlinear and linear evolutions nor Lyapunov stability of the origin. For a mechanical system with a configuration-dependent kinetic metric, the remainder hypothesis must be verified for the full first-order field (derivatives of $M$ and $M^{-1}$ included), not for the potential alone.
- **Averaging compares two different models.** [[thm-cm-averaging-for-fast-periodic-oscillations]] compares the solutions of $x'=\varepsilon f(t,x)$ and $y'=\varepsilon\bar f(y)$ and gives agreement of order $\varepsilon$ on the horizon $[0,A/\varepsilon]$ under the trapping condition $\varepsilon K<\rho$. The averaged equation is not equivalent to the oscillatory one; a longer horizon requires the trapping and smallness hypotheses to be checked again, and the theorem says nothing about stability or about invariant sets of the exact flow.
- **Adiabatic bounds need the chart, the frequency gap and the trapping.** [[thm-cm-adiabatic-invariant-drift-bound]] is conditional on a $C^2$ parameter-dependent action-angle datum with $|\partial_Ih|\ge\omega_0>0$ on the stated compact sets and on the branch solution staying in them. The existence of such a family for a given mechanical model, uniform in the parameter, is a separate hypothesis; resonances ($\omega=0$), separatrix crossings and action values leaving the chart are excluded, and the conclusion is a bound of order $\varepsilon$ on a finite rescaled-time horizon, not exact conservation of the action.

- **Downstream use.** Physical pages that read these results must adopt their own postulates and interpretations for masses, forces, damping, driving and adiabatic parameter variation, and must re-state the empirical qualifications of any measured input; none of the mathematics above supplies such interpretations.
items.strategy: Collect the hypotheses and limits of the preceding items in one place so that consumers carry them; no proof obligation is discharged by the remark.

items.title: Five worked initial value problems for the homogeneous oscillator across the discriminant, degenerate and repulsive cases
items.statement:
In each line, $m=1$ and the initial datum $(x_0,v_0)$ is prescribed for the homogeneous model with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and zero forcing, $x''+cx'+kx=0$ ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]). The solution is read off from the classification theorem and the degenerate-case proposition, and its initial values are checked explicitly.

- (i) $k=4$, $c=0$, $(x_0,v_0)=(1,0)$: the solution is $x(t)=\cos(2t)$.
- (ii) $k=1$, $c=2$, $(x_0,v_0)=(1,0)$: the solution is $x(t)=(1+t)e^{-t}$.
- (iii) $k=1$, $c=3$, $(x_0,v_0)=(1,0)$: with $\lambda_\pm=(-3\pm\sqrt5)/2$ the solution is $x(t)=\bigl(-\lambda_-e^{\lambda_+t}+\lambda_+e^{\lambda_-t}\bigr)/\sqrt5$.
- (iv) $k=0$, $c=2$, $(x_0,v_0)=(0,1)$: the solution is $x(t)=\tfrac12(1-e^{-2t})$.
- (v) $k=-1$, $c=0$, $(x_0,v_0)=(1,0)$: the solution is $x(t)=\tfrac12(e^{t}+e^{-t})$, which is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.
items.strategy: Compute the discriminant and coefficients from the classification theorem and the degenerate-case proposition and check the initial data explicitly.

items.title: Resonant forcing at $\Omega=\omega_0$ and the two regimes of the amplitude maximum
items.statement:
Consider the forced model $m\,x''+c\,x'+k\,x=f_0\cos(\Omega t)$ on time domain $I=\mathbb R$ with the values and conclusions below ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]], [[thm-cm-forced-oscillator-sinusoidal-response]], [[prop-cm-oscillator-amplitude-maximum]]).

- (i) Resonance: $m=k=f_0=1$, $c=0$, $\Omega=\omega_0=1$. Then $x_p(t)=\tfrac12t\sin t$ is a solution of $x''+x=\cos t$, it satisfies $x_p(0)=0$, $x_p'(0)=0$, and $|x_p|$ is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$.
- (ii) Amplitude peak above zero frequency: $m=k=f_0=1$, $c=1$. Then $u_*=1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12>0$, the maximum of $A(\Omega)=1/\sqrt{(1-\Omega^2)^2+\Omega^2}$ is attained at $\Omega_*=1/\sqrt2$, and $A(\Omega_*)=2/\sqrt3$, while $A(0)=A(1)=1$.
- (iii) Amplitude peak at zero frequency: $m=k=f_0=1$, $c=2$. Then $u_*=1-2=-1\le0$, and the maximum of $A(\Omega)=1/\sqrt{(1-\Omega^2)^2+4\Omega^2}$ on $[0,\infty)$ is attained at $\Omega=0$ with value $1$, while $A(1)=1/2$.
items.strategy: Substitute the resonant candidate using sine and cosine derivatives and evaluate the amplitude formula in the two regimes.

items.title: Constant forcing: free fall and the approach to terminal velocity under linear drag
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $g\in\mathbb R$ and consider the two constant-forcing models with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ (the half-line solution in (ii) is the restriction of its global solution) ([[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]]).

- (i) Uniform force: $x''=g$ with data $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$. The unique solution is $x(t)=x_0+v_0t+\tfrac12gt^2$.
- (ii) Linear drag: $m=1$, $c=2$, $g=1$, that is $x''+2x'=1$, with data $(x_0,v_0)=(0,0)$. The unique solution on $[0,\infty)$ is $x(t)=\tfrac12t-\tfrac14(1-e^{-2t})$, and its velocity $x'(t)=\tfrac12(1-e^{-2t})$ increases to the limiting value $\tfrac12$.
items.strategy: Read the solutions from the convolution representation with the explicit homogeneous kernels and differentiate.

items.title: Finite-time linearization bound for the planar pendulum with explicit constants
items.statement:
Let $l=g=1$ and consider the planar pendulum field

$$F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad F(\theta,\omega)=\bigl(\omega,\ -\sin\theta\bigr),$$

Let $\mathcal A:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2$ be the linear map $\mathcal A(\theta,\omega):=(\omega,-\theta)$, and let $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}\in M_2(\mathbb R)$ be its standard-coordinate matrix; use the matrix action of $A$ from [[thm-cm-finite-time-linearization-error-bound]]. On the closed ball $\overline B(0,\tfrac12)$ one has

$$\|F(z)-Az\|_2\le\tfrac1{12}\|z\|_2^2,\qquad \|F(z)\|_2\le\|z\|_2,$$

so the linearization theorem applies with $r=\tfrac12$, $C=\tfrac1{12}$, $L=1$. For the datum $z_0=(\tfrac1{100},0)$ and $T=1$ one has $\delta e^{LT}=\tfrac e{100}<\tfrac3{100}<\tfrac1{20}<\tfrac12$, and the theorem bounds the linearization error by

$$\|z(t)-y(t)\|_2\le\frac{\delta^2}{12}\int_0^1e^{(1-s)}e^{2s}\,ds<10^{-4}\qquad(0\le t\le1),$$

where $y$ solves $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$; in particular the linear solution stays within $10^{-4}$ of the nonlinear one on $[0,1]$.
items.strategy: Bound |sin theta - theta| by the Taylor remainder and |F(z)| by the norm of z, then substitute into the linearization theorem with ||A||=1.

The numerical pendulum bounds are calculated locally.

items.title: Averaging estimate on $[0,100]$ for the scalar equation $x'=\varepsilon\cos t$
items.statement:
Take $n=1$, $P=2\pi$, $O=\mathbb R$, $f(t,x)=\cos t$ (independent of $x$), $x_0=0$, and the trapping data $R=1$, $\rho=\tfrac12$, $A=1$. Then $f$ is continuous, $C^1$ in $x$ with $D_xf=0$, and $2\pi$-periodic in $t$; on $\mathbb R\times\overline B(0,1)$ one may take $M=1$ and $L=0$. The average and deviation of [[def-cm-averaging-data-and-averaged-field]] are

$$\bar f=0,\qquad g(t,x)=\sin t\quad(0\le t\le2\pi,\ \text{extended }2\pi\text{-periodically}).$$

The averaged system is $y'=0$, so $y(t)\equiv0$ solves it and stays in $\overline B(0,\tfrac12)$. With $B=2MP=4\pi$, $B_1=2LP=0$ and $K=e^{LA}[B+(LB+B_1M)A]=4\pi$, the smallness hypothesis reads $\varepsilon\cdot4\pi<\tfrac12$; for $\varepsilon=\tfrac1{100}$ it holds because $\varepsilon K=\tfrac{\pi}{25}<\tfrac12$. The averaging theorem then gives

$$|x(t)-y(t)|=|x(t)|\le\frac{\pi}{25}\qquad(0\le t\le100).$$

The exact solution is $x(t)=\tfrac1{100}\sin t$, whose modulus is at most $\tfrac1{100}$; the theorem's bound is valid but not sharp here.
items.strategy: Evaluate the averaging data and constants, verify the trapping hypotheses, and compare the theorem's bound with the exact solution.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.3, Eqs. (5.52)-(5.57): first-order averaging of a fast periodic term, printed pages 12-14 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 99-101)

I. Stewart, Advanced Classical Mechanics (MIT 8.09 Fall 2014, complete course text), Chapter 5 Sections 5.2-5.3, Eqs. (5.25)-(5.26): a perturbation whose one-period average vanishes produces only a periodic change, printed pages 96-97

items.title: An exactly solvable adiabatic branch: $K=I+\varepsilon I\cos\theta$ and comparison with the drift bound
items.statement:
Take $J=\mathbb R$, $S=\mathbb R$, $h(I,s)=I$ and $k(I,\theta,s)=I\cos\theta$ in the datum of [[def-cm-parameter-dependent-action-angle-branch]], with $\varepsilon=\tfrac1{10}$, $A=2$, $\omega_0=1$, $K=[6/5,19/10]$, $S_0=[0,2]$, $s_0=0$ and initial datum $I(0)=3/2$, $\theta(0)=0$. The branch system is

$$I'=\varepsilon I\sin\theta,\qquad \theta'=1+\varepsilon\cos\theta,\qquad s'=\varepsilon,$$

so $s(t)=\varepsilon t$ stays in $S_0=[0,2]$ on $[0,A/\varepsilon]=[0,20]$, and $I(t)$ stays in $K$ for all $t\ge0$. The quantity $J:=I(1+\varepsilon\cos\theta)$ is exactly invariant, the solution stays in $K\times S_0$ on $[0,A/\varepsilon]$, and

$$|I(t)-I(0)|\le\tfrac13\qquad(t\ge0),$$

while the drift bound of [[thm-cm-adiabatic-invariant-drift-bound]] evaluates in this instance to $|I(t)-I(0)|\le\tfrac{19}{50}$.
items.strategy: Exhibit the exact invariant of the branch system, verify trapping, and evaluate the theorem's constant (whose A-dependent term vanishes identically here).

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics, Classical Mechanics (complete 252-page volume), Chapter 10 Sections 10.2-10.3, Eqs. (10.28)-(10.42): action variable and adiabatic invariance, printed pages 5-8 of Chapter 10 (PDF pages 241-244)

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, January 2015 version), Section 4.6, Eqs. (4.150)-(4.158): the action $I=\frac1{2\pi}\oint p\,dq$ and the averaged invariance statement, printed pages 113-115

items.title: Continuity alone does not give uniqueness: $x'=\sqrt{|x|}$ through the origin
items.statement: Let $F:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Then for every $x_0\in\mathbb R$ the initial value problem $x'=F(x)$, $x(0)=x_0$ has at most one solution on every interval containing $0$.
items.strategy: Verify both solutions directly and conclude that the refuted uniqueness statement fails.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.2 (the Picard iteration and the role of the Lipschitz hypothesis; examples of nonunique solutions), printed pages 25-32

J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.2 (existence and uniqueness statements and the necessity of a Lipschitz condition), printed pages 12-21

items.title: A bounded field whose solution leaves the domain in finite time: $x'=v$, $v'=0$ on $(0,\infty)\times(-2,2)$
items.statement:
Let $U=(0,\infty)\times(-2,2)\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ and let $F:U\to\mathbb R^2$, $F(x,v)=(v,0)$, so that the first-order system $(x,v)'=F(x,v)$ is the free particle with velocity $v$ ([[def-cm-local-flow-of-an-autonomous-system]]). The solution of $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=(1,-1)$ is

$$z(t)=\bigl(x(t),v(t)\bigr)=(1-t,\ -1),\qquad t\in(-\infty,1).$$

Its maximal interval of existence is $(-\infty,1)$: at $t=1$ the position reaches the excluded boundary value $x=0$, although $\|F(x,v)\|=|v|<2$ is bounded on $U$ and the field extends smoothly to the plane. Hence a finite maximal interval does not require the field to blow up; the domain can force it.
items.strategy: Verify the explicit solution and show that no extension past t=1 can meet the domain condition.

references.title: G. Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS Graduate Studies in Mathematics 140, online edition), Section 2.1 and the blow-up examples of Chapter 2 (maximal domains are determined by the open domain of the field, not only by the size of the field), printed pages 17-24
J. Arino, MATH 8430 Fundamental Theory of Ordinary Differential Equations (University of Manitoba), Section 1.3 (maximal solutions and the role of the domain boundary), printed pages 22-30
